title: Working with Gemini
text:
Everything the app knows about a résumé, a job or a company comes from Google Gemini. All of that traffic goes through one class, GeminiService, in services/gemini_service.py. This page walks through what it sends, how it configures each request, and how it turns replies into Python data.
The examples run the real service code. At the very last step, where the service would send a request to Google, they replay saved replies instead, so the site builds without an API key and every build shows the same output.

title: Working with Gemini
text:
Setup

import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "..")

from services import gemini_service
from core.config import settings

gemini_service is created once, when services is first imported. Its constructor configures the Gemini client with settings.GEMINI_API_KEY and creates a model object. No request is sent at that point, so importing the app never needs network access.
The model and default parameters come from core/config.py:





Setting
Value




GEMINI_MODEL
gemini-flash-latest


GEMINI_TEMPERATURE
0.7


GEMINI_MAX_TOKENS
4096





All three can be overridden with environment variables or a .env file, because Settings is a pydantic BaseSettings class.






Note



The README says the app uses Gemini 1.5 Pro, but the configured model is gemini-flash-latest. The table above is read from the code, so it is the one to trust.

title: Working with Gemini
Working with Gemini
text:
From résumé to prompt
analyze_resume builds one long prompt: an instruction, the résumé text, the job description, and the exact JSON shape the reply must follow. Here is what it sends for a short résumé:

resume = "Jane Doe\nPython developer\nSkills: Python, FastAPI, SQL"

model = replay('{"overall_score": 7.5, "strengths": ["Python"], '
               '"skills_to_emphasize": [], "keywords_to_add": ["Docker"], '
               '"experience_to_highlight": [], "gaps_to_address": [], '
               '"improvement_areas": []}')

analysis = await gemini_service.analyze_resume(resume, job_role="Backend Engineer")
sent = model.requests[0]["prompt"]
print(sent[:420] + "\n...")

You are an expert resume analyst and career coach. Analyze this resume for a Backend Engineer position.

RESUME CONTENT:
Jane Doe
Python developer
Skills: Python, FastAPI, SQL

JOB DESCRIPTION:
No specific job description provided

Provide a comprehensive analysis in the following JSON format. YOUR ENTIRE RESPONSE MUST BE VALID JSON ONLY. DO NOT INCLUDE ANY TEXT OUTSIDE THE JSON STRUCTURE.

{
  "overall_score": 7.5,

...



assert "Backend Engineer position" in sent
assert resume in sent
assert "No specific job description provided" in sent
"✓ the prompt carries the role, the résumé, and a fallback job description"

'✓ the prompt carries the role, the résumé, and a fallback job description'


When no job description is given, the prompt says “No specific job description provided” rather than leaving the section empty. The reply comes back as a plain Python dictionary:

analysis

{'overall_score': 7.5,
 'strengths': ['Python'],
 'skills_to_emphasize': [],
 'keywords_to_add': ['Docker'],
 'experience_to_highlight': [],
 'gaps_to_address': [],
 'improvement_areas': []}

title: Working with Gemini
text:
Temperature for each task
Temperature controls how varied the model’s output is: low values give consistent, predictable text, high values give more creative text. The service picks a temperature per task. The table below is measured, not copied: each method is called and the temperature it actually sent is read back from the recorded request.





Method
Task
Temperature sent




analyze_resume
Résumé analysis
0.3


analyze_ats_compatibility
ATS check
0.3


research_company
Company research
0.3


generate_optimized_resume
Rewritten résumé
0.5


generate_cover_letter
Cover letter
0.7





Every method that expects JSON goes through generate_json_response, which fixes the temperature at 0.3 so replies stay close to the requested structure. The two writing tasks run warmer: 0.5 for the résumé, 0.7 for the cover letter.

A temperature of 0 is silently ignored
generate_content chooses its temperature with this line:
temperature=temperature or settings.GEMINI_TEMPERATURE,
In Python, 0.0 counts as false, so 0.0 or 0.7 evaluates to 0.7. Asking for the most deterministic output possible quietly gives the default instead:

model = replay("ok")
await gemini_service.generate_content("Say ok.", temperature=0.0)
model.requests[0]["config"].temperature

0.7



assert model.requests[0]["config"].temperature == settings.GEMINI_TEMPERATURE
"✓ confirmed: temperature=0.0 is replaced by the default"

'✓ confirmed: temperature=0.0 is replaced by the default'


No current caller passes 0.0, so the app’s output is not affected today. It would bite anyone who adds one. The fix is to test for None explicitly:
temperature=settings.GEMINI_TEMPERATURE if temperature is None else temperature,

title: Working with Gemini
text:
Turning replies into data
Language models do not always return clean JSON, even when told to. generate_json_response cleans the reply in three stages before giving up:

Strip Markdown code fences (```json at the start, ``` at the end).
Try to parse what is left as JSON.
If that fails, find the outermost { ... } in the text and parse only that.

Each case below sends a differently shaped reply through the real method:

async def parse(reply):
    replay(reply)
    return await gemini_service.generate_json_response("any prompt")

clean   = await parse('{"ats_score": 72}')
fenced  = await parse('```json\n{"ats_score": 72}\n```')
chatty  = await parse('Here is the analysis you asked for:\n{"ats_score": 72}\nGood luck!')
trailer = await parse('```json\n{"ats_score": 72}\n``` Hope this helps!')

clean, fenced, chatty, trailer

({'ats_score': 72}, {'ats_score': 72}, {'ats_score': 72}, {'ats_score': 72})



assert clean == fenced == chatty == trailer == {"ats_score": 72}
"✓ clean, fenced, chatty and trailing-text replies all parse to the same data"

'✓ clean, fenced, chatty and trailing-text replies all parse to the same data'


The last case is worth noticing. The closing fence is only stripped when it is the final thing in the reply, so Hope this helps! defeats stage 1 and the first parse fails. Stage 3 rescues it.
When there is no JSON object anywhere in the reply, the method raises:

try:
    await parse("Sorry, I can't help with that.")
except Exception as err:
    parse_error = str(err)

parse_error

'Failed to parse JSON response: Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0)'



assert parse_error.startswith("Failed to parse JSON response")
"✓ a reply with no JSON raises a labelled error"

'✓ a reply with no JSON raises a labelled error'

title: Working with Gemini
text:
When the request itself fails
Any error from the Gemini client (a bad key, no network, an exhausted quota) is caught and re-raised with a Gemini API error: prefix:

class FailingModel:
    def generate_content(self, prompt, generation_config=None):
        raise RuntimeError("API key not valid")

gemini_service.model = FailingModel()
try:
    await gemini_service.generate_content("hello")
except Exception as err:
    api_error = str(err)

api_error

'Gemini API error: API key not valid'



assert api_error == "Gemini API error: API key not valid"
"✓ client errors are wrapped with a clear prefix"

'✓ client errors are wrapped with a clear prefix'


As with the PDF service, the error is re-raised as a plain Exception, so the original error type is lost. The API routers catch it and return HTTP 500, adding their own prefix, so a client sees a detail such as “Error analyzing resume: Gemini API error: API key not valid”.

Things to know when changing this service:

Replies are not validated here. Whatever keys Gemini returns are passed on as-is; checking the shape is left to the API layer’s response models.
temperature=0.0 is replaced by the default (see above).
All failures surface as plain Exceptions, distinguished only by message.

title: About
text:
About these docs
This site is written in Quarto. Pages are .qmd files: Markdown with Python code cells that run during every build. The site imports the app from the repository root and documents what the code actually does, not what it was meant to do.
Three rules keep the pages trustworthy:

Every claim is checked. Pages end their examples with assert statements. If the app’s behaviour changes, an assertion fails, and Quarto stops the build instead of publishing a wrong page.
No network, no keys. Pages that involve Gemini use a stand-in model with fixed replies. Builds are free, identical every time, and need no GEMINI_API_KEY.
No side effects. Sample PDFs are generated during the build, and any files the app writes go to temporary folders, never to uploads/ or outputs/.

title: About
text:
Building the site
The docs have their own Python environment, managed with uv. It pins the app’s own dependencies from requirements.txt, plus the documentation tools (jupyter, fpdf2, httpx).
cd docs
uv sync                    # install the environment
uv run quarto preview      # live preview while writing
uv run quarto render       # build the site into _site/
uv run matters: it puts this project’s Python first on the PATH, so Quarto runs the cells with the right packages installed.

title: Job Application Optimizer
text:
The Job Application Optimizer takes a PDF résumé and a job description, and uses Google Gemini to tell you how well the two match, what to change, and what to expect from the company. It can then write a tailored résumé and cover letter as Word documents.
These pages document how the backend works. Every code example on them is run against the real code in this repository when the site is built, so what you read is what the code does today.

title: Job Application Optimizer
text:
What it does








Step
What happens
Where in the code




1. Upload
Text is extracted from the résumé PDF
services/pdf_service.py


2. Analyse
Gemini scores the résumé (1–10) against the job role
services/gemini_service.py


3. ATS check
Gemini estimates an applicant-tracking-system score (0–100%) and lists missing keywords
services/gemini_service.py


4. Research
Gemini summarises the target company
services/gemini_service.py


5. Recommend
The analyses above are combined into interview and application advice
services/gemini_service.py


6. Generate
A rewritten résumé and a cover letter are saved as .docx files
services/document_service.py

title: Job Application Optimizer
text:
How the pieces fit
A React frontend talks to a FastAPI backend over HTTP. The backend’s routers are thin: they validate input and hand the work to three services.





flowchart LR
  UI["React frontend<br/>(frontend/)"] -->|HTTP| API["FastAPI routers<br/>(api/)"]
  API --> PDF["pdf_service<br/>PyPDF2"]
  API --> GEM["gemini_service<br/>Google Gemini"]
  API --> DOC["document_service<br/>python-docx"]
  GEM -->|prompts| CLOUD[("Gemini API")]
  DOC --> OUT[/"outputs/*.docx"/]

title: Job Application Optimizer
text:
Running it locally
git clone https://github.com/Dharundp6/AI_resume_Reviewer-.git
cd AI_resume_Reviewer-
pip install -r requirements.txt
cd frontend && npm install && cd ..
echo GEMINI_API_KEY=your_key_here > .env
python app.py          # backend on http://localhost:8000
The frontend runs separately with npm start inside frontend/, on http://localhost:3000. Every step except the upload needs a Gemini API key. That includes document generation: Gemini writes the résumé and cover letter, and python-docx only formats them.

title: Reading a résumé PDF
text:
Every analysis in the app starts from plain text. When someone uploads a résumé, the first job is to pull the text out of the PDF. That job belongs to pdf_service, defined in services/pdf_service.py.
Everything on this page is executed against the real code when the site is built. If the service changes behaviour, the checks below fail and the build stops.

title: Reading a résumé PDF
text:
Setup
The app’s modules import each other by top-level name (from services import ..., from core.config import settings), so Python needs the repository root on its module search path before anything can be imported:

import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "..")

from services import pdf_service
from services.pdf_service import PDFService

pdf_service is a ready-made instance of the PDFService class. Both of its methods are static, so the instance holds no state; it exists so the rest of the app can import one shared object.

title: Reading a résumé PDF
text:
Building sample résumés
Rather than depend on a real CV, the page generates its own PDFs at build time. This keeps the docs reproducible on any machine and free of personal data.

from fpdf import FPDF

def make_pdf(*pages: str) -> bytes:
    """Build a PDF with one page per string argument."""
    pdf = FPDF()
    pdf.set_font("Helvetica", size=12)
    for page_text in pages:
        pdf.add_page()
        if page_text:
            pdf.multi_cell(0, 8, page_text)
    return bytes(pdf.output())

one_page = make_pdf("Jane Doe\nPython developer\nSkills: Python, FastAPI, SQL")
f"{len(one_page):,} bytes"

'1,033 bytes'

title: Reading a résumé PDF
text:
The two methods








Method
Takes
Used by




extract_text_from_pdf(file)
an open binary file object
the other method


extract_text_from_bytes(pdf_bytes)
raw bytes
the /api/resume/upload endpoint



The upload endpoint receives the file as bytes, so it calls extract_text_from_bytes, which wraps the bytes in an in-memory file (io.BytesIO) and hands them to extract_text_from_pdf.

title: Reading a résumé PDF
text:
Extracting a one-page résumé

text = pdf_service.extract_text_from_bytes(one_page)
print(text)

Jane Doe
Python developer
Skills: Python, FastAPI, SQL


The result has 3 lines. The check below confirms the text comes back exactly as it went in:

assert text == "Jane Doe\nPython developer\nSkills: Python, FastAPI, SQL"
"✓ extraction matches the input"

'✓ extraction matches the input'

title: Reading a résumé PDF
text:
Multi-page résumés
The service extracts each page separately, joins them with a blank line ("\n\n"), then strips whitespace from both ends:

two_pages = make_pdf("Page one: experience", "Page two: education")
multi = pdf_service.extract_text_from_bytes(two_pages)
print(repr(multi))

'Page one: experience\n\nPage two: education'



assert multi == "Page one: experience\n\nPage two: education"
"✓ pages are joined with a blank line"

'✓ pages are joined with a blank line'


The blank line matters downstream: it is the only marker of where one page ends and the next begins once the text reaches Gemini.

title: Reading a résumé PDF
section: When the input is not a PDF
text:
When the input is not a PDF
If the bytes are not a readable PDF, the service catches the underlying PyPDF2 error and re-raises it as a plain Exception with a readable prefix:

try:
    pdf_service.extract_text_from_bytes(b"this is not a pdf")
except Exception as err:
    error_message = str(err)

print(error_message)

Failed to extract text from PDF: EOF marker not found



assert error_message.startswith("Failed to extract text from PDF:")
"✓ bad input raises a clearly labelled error"

'✓ bad input raises a clearly labelled error'


Because it is re-raised as a plain Exception, callers cannot tell a corrupt file apart from any other failure by exception type; they only have the message text.

title: Reading a résumé PDF
section: When the PDF has no text
text:
When the PDF has no text
A PDF made only of images (a scanned CV, for example) contains no text layer. Extraction does not fail; it returns an empty string:

blank = pdf_service.extract_text_from_bytes(make_pdf(""))
repr(blank)

"''"



assert blank == ""
"✓ a PDF with no text layer gives an empty string"

'✓ a PDF with no text layer gives an empty string'


The service leaves that case to its caller. The upload endpoint in api/resume.py checks for it and responds with HTTP 400 “No text could be extracted from the PDF”. The app has no OCR step, so scanned résumés cannot be analysed.
